title: Is a new customer worth it?
principle: Each customer must earn more margin than winning them cost.

screens.text: Let me tell you about PepperTap, an Indian grocery delivery app that started in 2014. It gave big discounts to win buyers. In 2015, it claimed 40,000 orders in a single day. In April 2016, it shut down.

screens.prompt: It had so many orders. Why do you think PepperTap shut down?

options.label: Rivals copied its app and its prices
It lost money on every order it won

screens.why: Its boss said it was losing cash on every order. Discounts and the high cost of winning customers ate the money. Orders fell to about 7,000 or 8,000 a day, and it closed.

screens.title: LTV:CAC
screens.text: What one customer costs to win is your spend divided by the customers it brought: ₹6,000 for 20 is ₹300 each. That's customer acquisition cost, or CAC. Compare it with lifetime value, LTV. Investors call this LTV:CAC. If LTV isn't well above CAC, growth makes you poorer.

screens.prompt: You spend ₹3,000 on Instagram ads, and 10 new families order. What did each family cost to win?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹3,000 ÷ 10 families = ₹300 each. That's your CAC.

wrong.b: ₹3,000 is what you spent on all 10 families. Divide by 10: ₹300 each.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Last lesson, loops beat paying for each buyer. But paying is fine when each buyer earns back more than they cost. Let's check your bakery. It's June. A family who stays usually orders 4 cakes a year, and each cake leaves you ₹450.

screens.prompt: A new family cost ₹600 to win. Each cake leaves you ₹450. After how many cakes have you earned back the ₹600?
screens.why: Right. One cake leaves ₹450, still ₹150 short. The second cake makes ₹900, more than ₹600. This is the payback: how many orders before a customer repays what you spent to win them.

wrong.a: One cake leaves ₹450, but you spent ₹600, so you're still ₹150 short. After 2 cakes you have ₹900, so the payback is 2 cakes.
wrong.c: You're there sooner: 2 cakes leave ₹900, more than the ₹600 you spent. The payback is 2 cakes.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six ways you won families last year. For each one, tell me: did it earn back more than it cost?

items.text: ₹300 of ads; the family stays and orders 4 cakes a year
₹500 of free samples; the family orders one ₹450-margin cake
A ₹5 card in a box; the family orders 4 cakes a year
₹2,000 to a blogger; 2 families order once each
₹100 of referral discounts; the family orders 4 cakes a year
₹1,000 coupon; the family orders 2 cakes in all

screens.why: Good sorting. Ads, the card and referrals cost far less than the families earned back. The samples, the blogger and the big coupon cost more than ₹450 for each cake sold.

screens.prompt: Ads win families at ₹300 each. Each is worth about ₹9,000 over five years. You have ₹30,000. Why not spend it all now?

options.label: The ₹9,000 comes over years; the cash goes now
₹300 is too much for one family
Ads always stop working after a month

screens.why: Exactly. Remember Unit 1: businesses die when cash runs out. Each family pays you back slowly, cake by cake. Spend in steps, and let early payback fund the next round.

wrong.b: ₹300 is cheap next to ₹9,000. The problem is timing. Remember Unit 1: you spend the ₹30,000 now, but the ₹9,000 comes over five years. Cash can run out first.
wrong.c: We don't know that. The problem is timing. Remember Unit 1: you spend the ₹30,000 now, but the ₹9,000 comes over five years. Cash can run out first.

screens.setup: It's late June. You have ₹6,000 to win new families before the festival months. A family who stays usually orders 4 cakes a year. Each cake leaves you ₹450.
screens.question: Where do you spend the ₹6,000?

options.label: ₹300 off the first cake, for anyone on your menu
options.outcome: 20 orders use the coupon, but 14 come from your old families. Only 6 families are new, so each new one cost you ₹1,000. Their first cakes leave you just ₹150 each.
options.why: Your old customers took most of the discount. Divide the cost by new families only, and the CAC was ₹1,000.
options.better: Boost Instagram reels, where a new family costs you about ₹300.

options.label: Boost Instagram reels with the ₹6,000
options.outcome: The reels bring 20 new families: ₹300 each. Each family's first cake leaves you ₹450, so they pay back on the first order. If they stay a year, each one leaves you ₹1,800.
options.why: CAC of ₹300 against ₹1,800 a year of margin, with payback on the first cake. The numbers say yes.

options.label: Pay a food blogger ₹6,000 for one big post
options.outcome: The post looks lovely and brings 8 new families: ₹750 each. Each needs two cakes to pay back. Some only order once.
options.why: It can still pay over time, but each family cost more than twice as much as the reels did.
options.better: Boost Instagram reels, where a new family costs you about ₹300.

screens.text: Divide what you ___ by the new customers it brought. Each customer must earn more ___ than that.
screens.why: Exactly. That's LTV:CAC. Your reels won families at ₹300 each, and each one leaves you ₹1,800 a year.

summary: CAC: what you spent to win customers ÷ the new customers it brought.
LTV:CAC: lifetime value must be well above CAC, or growth makes you poorer.
Payback: how many orders before a customer repays their CAC. Long paybacks can empty your cash.

cards.front: ₹6,000 of ads brought 20 new customers. What's the CAC?
A customer costs ₹500 to win and orders once, leaving ₹200. Worth it?
options: Yes, a sale is a sale
cards.back: Each customer must earn more margin than winning them cost.

cards.front: A customer costs ₹600 to win. Each order leaves ₹300. What's the payback?
cards.back: ₹300 × 2 = ₹600. Paid back on the second order.
